t-6.5-outputs.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule (continued): agile release planning, schedule baseline, schedule presentations, schedule data, calendars
t-6.5-outputs.notes: PMIS scheduling software generates start and finish dates from activities, network diagrams, resources and durations. Agile release planning: a high-level summary timeline of the release schedule (typically 3 to 6 months) based on the product roadmap and vision; determines the number of iterations or sprints in the release; lets the product owner and team decide how much to build and how long until a releasable product, given business goals, dependencies and impediments; features represent customer value, so the timeline shows which features will be available at the end of each iteration. Figure 6-20 hierarchy: product vision drives the product roadmap; the roadmap drives release plans; a release plan establishes the iterations; iteration plans schedule feature development; prioritised features are delivered by user stories estimated in story points; tasks to deliver stories are estimated in hours. Outputs: schedule baseline - approved version of the schedule model with baseline start and finish dates, changed only via formal change control, compared to actuals during M&C, a plan component. Project schedule - output of the schedule model presenting linked activities with planned dates, durations, milestones and resources; at minimum planned start and finish for each activity; preliminary until resource assignments are confirmed (usually no later than completion of the project management plan); a target schedule may also exist; summary (master/milestone schedule) or detailed. Presentations: bar (Gantt) charts - activities on the vertical axis, dates on the horizontal axis, bars for durations; easy to read; summary activities for control communications; milestone charts - only start/completion of major deliverables and key external interfaces; project schedule network diagrams - activity-on-node without time scale ('pure logic diagram') or time-scaled ('logic bar chart'/time-scaled logic diagram) showing logic and critical path. Figure 6-21 shows a milestone schedule, a summary schedule and a detailed schedule for 'New Product Z' with a data date. Schedule data - at minimum milestones, activities, activity attributes and documented assumptions and constraints; often resource histograms, alternative schedules (best/worst case, leveled or not, with or without imposed dates), applied schedule reserves, cash-flow projections, order and delivery schedules. Project calendars - working days and shifts available; a model may need several. Change requests (incl. preventive actions to reduce the probability of negative schedule variance). Plan updates: schedule management plan, cost baseline. Document updates: activity attributes, assumption log, duration estimates, lessons learned, resource requirements (leveling may change them), risk register.

t-6.6-control-schedule.title: 6.6 Control Schedule: predictive and agile control, burndown charts, variance on critical vs non-critical paths, schedule forecasts
t-6.6-control-schedule.notes: Monitor project status to update the schedule and manage changes to the schedule baseline; key benefit: baseline maintained; performed throughout. Updating the model requires actual performance; any change to the schedule baseline must be approved through Perform Integrated Change Control. Concerns: current schedule status; influencing factors that create schedule changes; reconsidering schedule reserves; determining if the schedule has changed; managing actual changes. Agile: compare total work delivered and accepted with estimates for the elapsed cycle; retrospectives (scheduled reviews recording lessons to correct and improve processes); reprioritise the backlog; determine velocity (rate deliverables are produced, validated and accepted per iteration of agreed length, typically 2 weeks or 1 month); determine changes; manage changes. For contracted work, regular and milestone status updates from contractors plus status reviews and walkthroughs to verify contractor reports. Inputs: plan (schedule management plan - update frequency, reserve use, control approach; schedule baseline; scope baseline; performance measurement baseline); documents (lessons learned, project calendars, project schedule - latest version with notations, resource calendars, schedule data); work performance data (activities started, progress - actual duration, remaining duration, physical percent complete - and finished); OPAs (schedule control policies, tools, monitoring and reporting methods). Tools: data analysis - earned value analysis (SV and SPI), iteration burndown chart (tracks work remaining in the iteration backlog against an ideal diagonal burndown from iteration planning; plot daily actual remaining work; a trend line forecasts completion and likely variance), performance reviews (actual start/finish dates, percent complete, remaining duration vs baseline), trend analysis, variance analysis (planned vs actual dates, durations and float; cause and degree of variance; implications for remaining work; e.g., a long delay on a non-critical activity may matter little while a short delay on a critical or near-critical activity may need immediate action), what-if scenario analysis guided by risk outputs; critical path method (progress on the critical path determines status; critical-path variance directly affects the end date; near-critical paths reveal schedule risk); PMIS; resource optimisation; leads and lags (e.g., increase lead so landscaping starts before exterior work finishes; remove lag so editing starts right after writing); schedule compression (fast tracking or crashing remaining work). Source note: Figure 6-22 numbers the tools .1-.4 then .6-.7 (no .5) - a numbering gap in the source figure; the overview Figure 6-1 lists the same six tools. Outputs: work performance information (variances in dates and durations at work package and control account level; SV and SPI for work performance reports); schedule forecasts (estimates or predictions of future conditions based on current knowledge, past performance and expected corrective/preventive actions; can include EV indicators and schedule reserve information); change requests; plan updates (schedule management plan; schedule baseline - for approved changes in scope, resources or duration estimates, or changes caused by compression or performance issues; cost baseline; performance measurement baseline); document updates (assumption log, basis of estimates, lessons learned, project schedule, resource calendars, risk register - risks from compression, schedule data - possibly a new target schedule when delays are severe). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPI and schedule forecasts to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

c-cost-overview.title: Project Cost Management overview: four processes, life-cycle cost, measuring cost, earned schedule trend, tailoring, agile
c-cost-overview.section: 7 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 7-1)
c-cost-overview.notes: Planning, estimating, budgeting, financing, funding, managing and controlling costs so the project completes within the approved budget. Processes: 7.1 Plan Cost Management (how costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored, controlled); 7.2 Estimate Costs (approximation of monetary resources needed); 7.3 Determine Budget (aggregate estimated costs of activities or work packages into an authorised cost baseline); 7.4 Control Costs (monitor status, update costs, manage changes to the cost baseline). On small projects estimating and budgeting may be one process. The ability to influence cost is greatest early in the project, so early scope definition is critical. Key concepts: primarily the cost of resources to complete activities, but also consider effects of project decisions on recurring costs of using, maintaining and supporting the product (life-cycle costing - e.g., fewer design reviews may cut project cost but raise operating cost). Stakeholders measure cost differently and at different times (when committed, ordered, delivered, or incurred/recorded). Predicting the product's financial performance (ROI, discounted cash flow, payback) is often outside the project, but may be included (e.g., capital facilities). Trend: earned schedule (ES) extends EVM - replaces SV = EV - PV with SV = ES - AT (actual time); if ES - AT is greater than 0 the project is ahead of schedule; SPI = ES / AT; also forecasts completion dates from ES, AT and estimated duration. (Source wording says 'if the amount of earned schedule is greater than 0'; the lesson will state the comparison as ES - AT > 0 and flag the wording.) Tailoring: knowledge management and financial databases, estimating and budgeting policies, use of EVM, agile approaches, governance. Agile: with high uncertainty or undefined scope, detailed cost calculations may not pay off; use lightweight estimation for a fast high-level labour cost forecast, detailed estimates just-in-time for short horizons; under strict budgets, scope and schedule are adjusted to stay within cost. ITTOs for 7.1-7.4 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 7-1.

c-7.1-plan-cost.title: 7.1 Plan Cost Management: the cost management plan
c-7.1-plan-cost.notes: Define how costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored and controlled; key benefit: guidance on cost management; once or at predefined points; occurs early and sets the framework for the other cost processes. Inputs: charter (preapproved financial resources; approval requirements); plan (schedule management plan, risk management plan - both affect estimation and management); EEFs (culture and structure, market conditions, currency exchange rates, published commercial cost-rate information and seller price lists, PMIS, regional productivity differences); OPAs (financial controls procedures - time reporting, expenditure reviews, accounting codes, contract provisions; historical information; financial databases; estimating and budgeting policies). Tools: expert judgment (similar projects, industry information, estimating and budgeting, EVM); alternatives analysis (strategic funding options - self-funding, equity, debt; ways to acquire resources - make, purchase, rent, lease); meetings. Output: cost management plan - units of measure (hours, days, weeks; metres, litres, tons, cubic yards; lump sum in currency); level of precision (rounding, e.g., US$995.59 to US$1,000); level of accuracy (acceptable range such as +/-10%, may include contingency); organisational procedures links (WBS framework; the control account is the WBS component used for project cost accounting, with a code linking to the organisation's accounting system); control thresholds (agreed % variation before action); rules of performance measurement (where in the WBS control accounts are measured; EVM techniques such as weighted milestones, fixed-formula, percent complete; tracking methods and EVM equations for EAC forecasts as a validity check on the bottom-up EAC); reporting formats; additional details (strategic funding choices, currency fluctuation procedure, cost recording procedure).
